text.en: A seed and a small stone look alike. Plant both in soil with water. After a week the seed sprouts. The stone does not. What makes something alive?

Living things share certain characteristics. They need food, they breathe, they grow, they respond to changes, they reproduce and they die. A stone or a toy does not show these characteristics, so it is non-living.
Living things need water, a source of energy and surroundings that meet their needs. Plants and animals also exchange gases with their surroundings. Plants make their own food using sunlight. Animals get food by eating plants or other animals.
A seed needs water, air and a suitable temperature to germinate, which means to sprout. In a typical bean seedling, the root grows downward and the shoot grows upward. Roots and shoots keep growing after the seedling emerges. Plants respond to light, and many plant parts grow toward it. Touch-me-not leaves fold when touched.
A flowering plant can grow from seed to seedling to adult plant. A flower may become a fruit containing new seeds, and the cycle can begin again. Many animals change form as they grow. A butterfly goes from egg to caterpillar to pupa to butterfly. A frog goes from egg to tadpole to frog. A mosquito goes from egg to larva to pupa to adult, and these early stages live in water.
Living things respond to stimuli like light, sound, touch and temperature. They reproduce to make more of their kind and all living things eventually die.

Compare a rolling ball, a pebble and a seedling. The ball moves after a push, the pebble stays still and a new leaf grows on the seedling. To decide which is living, look for several life processes over time.

board.text: Rolling ball: moved by a push

text.en: Some animals move from place to place. A rooted plant can also move its growing parts or close its leaves. A plant can show life processes even while it remains in the same spot.

board.text: Movement can happen in part of a plant

text.en: Plants and animals release energy from food through respiration. Cells in a growing root need energy too, just as cells in a running animal do.

board.text: Roots and muscles contain living cells

text.en: Living things also get rid of wastes made inside their bodies. This is called excretion. The carbon dioxide animals breathe out is one example.

board.text: Excretion removes wastes made in the body

text.en: Take a look at two beans. One has put out a root, while the dry one still looks unchanged. A dry seed may be alive but resting. We can look for evidence that it starts growing under suitable conditions.
To see what changes a seed can make in a few days, mark the day on a sketch and draw the first root once it appears. Keep the sketch series so you can compare changes across days.
Compare two drawings of the same kind of bean seed. One is on a damp pad and one is on a dry pad. If warmth and air are the same, water is the condition that differs.

board.text: Same kind of seed, warmth and air

text.en: A waterlogged pad may leave too little air around the bean. A moist pad gives a seed water while gaps around it still contain air. Both conditions matter during germination.

board.text: Moist pad: water and access to air
Soaked pad: less access to air

text.en: A bean can begin germinating using food already stored in its seed. Later the seedling unfolds leaves, and light allows those leaves to make food for continued growth.

board.text: Leaves use light to make food later

text.en: Watch a healthy potted plant from two directions and you may see a shoot bend toward a bright window. The light is a stimulus and the change in the direction of growth is a response.

board.text: Shoot bending as it grows: response

text.en: Compare that slow bend with a sensitive plant folding its leaves after a touch. The stimulus and the speed of the response differ even though both are responses.
Follow the stages of a bean plant on the board. A pod can hold seeds. When a new bean germinates and grows into a plant that makes pods, it continues the life cycle.
One bean plant eventually dies and another can grow from its seeds. Reproduction continues a kind of living thing across generations.
Picture a frog egg in water, then a tadpole with a long tail. Many tadpoles grow legs and gradually lose the tail as they change into young frogs.
Compare the two frog drawings. The tadpole picture should show a long tail suited to swimming. The young frog picture should show legs and a much smaller tail or no tail.

board.text: Young frog: legs and a smaller tail

text.en: Use a picture sequence to identify the four stages of a mosquito. An egg comes first, followed by a larva, a pupa and an adult. The adult has wings.
Compare the two animal cycles. Both change form across their life cycles. A frog does not have the pupa stage shown in the mosquito diagram.

board.text: Same idea: change across the life cycle
Pupa appears in the mosquito cycle

text.en: A plant near a window has grown taller and turned toward the light. Which clue shows growth, and which clue shows response? Explain what each observation tells you about the plant.
It uses oxygen and gives heat, but does it grow, respond and reproduce?
It does not, so a flame is not living.

prompt.en: Explain how you would prove that a seed is living.

requiredIdeas.en: Plant it with water and air.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking moving things are always living.
Thinking a plant does not respond.

points.en: Living things need food, breathe, grow, respond, reproduce and die.
Seeds need water, air and warmth to germinate.
Life cycles can include big changes in form.
